title: N.L. premier waiting to hear from Quebec on Churchill River power deal
summary: Quebec Energy Minister Stéphane Paquet said the Churchill River power deal is not set in stone, setting off a series of questions for Premier Tony Wakeham in Newfoundland and Labrador's House of…

image.caption: Premier Tony Wakeham has again told Newfoundland and Labrador's House of Assembly he's not prepared to entertain re-opening of the material terms in a standing energy deal between electrical utilities in Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

Quebec Energy Minister Stéphane Paquet said the Churchill River power deal is not set in stone, setting off a series of questions for Premier Tony Wakeham in Newfoundland and Labrador's House of Assembly.
Wakeham says he's not prepared to change material terms in standing agreement
Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham said Monday he hasn't heard anything from the new Quebec government about the Churchill River power deal being "not set in stone."
That's despite Quebec Energy Minister Stéphane Paquet sharing the thought in an interview with Montreal talk radio station 98.5FM Friday morning.

Paquet said the new government has reviewed the non-binding agreement signed to date by provincial power utilities — known as the Definitive Cooperation and Implementation Agreement (DCIA). The agreement was the subject of a special debate in the legislature in Newfoundland and Labrador this fall.

"And now, upon analysis, yes, there are things we don’t agree with, so we’re going to work with our friends in Newfoundland to ensure that certain clauses in there satisfy everyone," Paquet said in French, on the radio program.
The interviewer then asked Quebec's minister if the power deal was set in stone.
"This deal is not set in stone," Paquet replied.

items: Churchill River energy agreement with Quebec not open for renegotiation, says N.L.

blocks.text: It all came up in Question Period in the Newfoundland and Labrador legislature on Monday, with questions from Liberal Leader John Hogan and NDP MHA Sheilagh O'Leary.

"Again, the reality is Quebec is in a different place than Newfoundland and Labrador and we’re hearing things different than what this Premier is telling people in our province," Hogan said on the floor, before accusing the premier of hiding what's happening with the multi-billion dollar power sales and infrastructure agreement.
Wakeham said he'd spoken with Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. He also said Newfoundland and Labrador's position was clearly communicated: material terms in the deal won't be touched.
"The deal will not be renegotiated," the premier told the House.

Just outside the legislature, he said the negotiating teams are back together, working to finalize contracts, and he has nothing from Quebec saying the leadership wants to go back to re-negotiate anything in the DCIA.
"We have reached an agreement. A deal is done," Wakeham repeated, describing the ongoing work as simply turning the material terms into final contracts.
He said work is ongoing to arrange a meeting in person with St-Pierre Plamondon.
Liberal Leader John Hogan speaks to reporters outside the House of Assembly in St. John's on Nov. 16, 2026. (CBC)

The Liberals said any request to re-open the DCIA terms could be seen as an opportunity for Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro and the premier to "get it right," reiterating the position what's in the existing agreement isn't right for the province long term.

"He continues to say he's confident and comfortable with the deal. If he's so confident and comfortable, why can't he bring the final agreements to the House of Assembly [when completed], so Newfoundlanders and Labradorians can see it, we can debate it and we can have a vote on it to make sure it is the right deal for our entire province for now and for the next 50 years," Hogan said to reporters.
Wakeham is not planning to return to the legislature with final contracts before they are signed.
As for the idea of Quebec re-negotiating key terms?
"Our premier did it. I think it'd be pretty rich for him to turn around and say the Quebec premier can't do it," Hogan said.
